_meta.description: Positioning. Expressions grouped by conviction cluster, each tagged with the limb it expresses and the falsifier that would retire it. Sizing logic, entry discipline, the deliberate internal hedges, and what is explicitly not owned.
_meta.status: Framework and candidate list. Not a live book — no weights, no cost basis, no recommendation.
_meta.review_note: Every position must name the falsifier that retires it. A position with no falsifier is a view, not a trade.

defining_insight.title: Own the gradient, not the direction
defining_insight.body: Everyone knows the population is aging. The consensus expression — senior housing REITs and large-cap medtech — is fully narrativised and priced. The edge, if there is one, sits in three places the consensus flattens. First, the gradient: businesses paid by the 65-74 band face a population that peaks around 2030 and then declines, while those paid by 75+ have a tailwind past 2040, and the market prices them as one theme. Second, the labour limb: nobody is positioned for aging to be inflationary. Third, structure: the same demographics that guarantee healthcare volume make healthcare price the most politically exposed line in the budget, so the entire care book should be built on volume and private-pay rather than on reimbursement rates holding.

clusters.title: Core — highest conviction, thesis-defining
clusters.body: Positions where the mechanism is strongest, the crowding lowest, or both. Each expresses a limb the consensus is not positioned for.
items: Capacity gap in licensed labour (limb C): CVSA — owns accredited nursing capacity in a pipeline that turns away qualified applicants. The purest way to own limb C's binding constraint rather than its symptom. Falsifier: programme capacity expanding faster than the 85+ population.

Private-pay age curves (limb D): ALC, SOON.SW — cataract and hearing are biologically inevitable, high-penetration-upside, and structurally outside reimbursement risk. The rarest combination in the universe. Falsifier: OTC or direct-to-consumer channels collapsing the private-pay premium.

Structural heart (limb D): EW — aortic stenosis prevalence rises steeply past 75 and TAVR converts inoperable into routine. Volume-driven, not price-driven. Falsifier: competitive share loss in structural heart, not demand.

Care operating competence (limb D): ENSG, ADUS — the demand is arithmetic; the scarce skill is managing care labour at Medicaid rates. Own the operators who have demonstrated it. Falsifier: a Medicaid rate reset, or caregiver wage inflation outrunning rate growth.
Income manufacturing (limb A): EQH, CRBG, APO — retiree money changes wrapper rather than leaving. Own the wrapper. Falsifier: sustained net equity outflow from the 65+ cohort in the flow data.
Intermediation shift (limb B): LPLA, MS — two break points per estate plus an aging advisor population. Falsifier: wirehouse retention of heir relationships improving.

Terminal certainty (limb B/D): SCI — the one demand curve that cannot be deferred, substituted or reformed away, pre-funded by a preneed backlog. Falsifier: cremation mix eroding revenue per case faster than volume grows.

clusters.title: Engaged — right thesis, waiting on price or evidence
clusters.body: The mechanism holds but the entry does not, or a key operating metric has yet to confirm. These are the names the alert engine is watching for a drawdown.
items: Skilled-labour contractors: EME, FIX, PWR — the labour-scarcity moat is genuine and durable, but the price embeds a datacentre construction cycle. You are not being paid to take the demographic risk here. Wait for a cycle scare.

Senior housing supply trough: WELL, VTR, BKD — the cyclical setup is real. The problem is that it is the single most consensus expression of the whole thesis, and limb C eats the incremental revenue. Watch occupancy and operating margin together, never occupancy alone.
Hearing breadth: DEMANT.CO, AMP.MI, COH.AX — same curve as Sonova at different points on the value chain and the valuation range.
Orthopaedic volume: SYK, ZBH — volume grows, price per implant erodes. The thesis needs volume to outrun price; a decade of ZBH share loss says execution decides it.
Pharmacy distribution: MCK, COR — slow, reliable, volume-not-price, structurally insulated from limb E. Boring in the way this thesis should like.
Net-lease care real estate: CTRE, OHI — being the landlord rather than the operator is the deliberate answer to limb C. Paid to wait, which answers weakness w1.
Trade training: LINC, UTI — employer-pulled enrolment into the trades shortage. Small, regulatory-exposed, direct.

clusters.title: Fade — right demography, expiring clock
clusters.body: Businesses paid by the go-go band. The population supporting them peaks around 2030 and then declines. Fade into strength rather than shorting — earnings roll over after the demography does, not with it, and the interval can be years.
items: VIK — the most precisely targeted business in the universe, serving a band that stops growing. Its competitive advantage is its refusal to serve anyone else, which is exactly the problem.
RCL, CCL — broader mixes give partial insulation; the core customer still skews to the expiring band, on cycle-peak earnings and multiples.
THO, BC, GOLF — RVs, boats and golf are go-go behaviours with hard biological limits. Cheap cyclicals, not thesis longs.
STMN.SW — private-pay and age-driven, but genuinely discretionary. A wealth-effect trade wearing a demographic costume.
PHM, TMHC — active-adult builders have a real rate-insensitivity advantage from equity-rich buyers, and a visible expiry on the tailwind.

clusters.title: Deliberate internal hedges
clusters.body: Positions held specifically because they profit if part of the thesis is wrong. These are not diversification — each one is matched to a named falsifier.
items: LLY against limb D's falsifier: the GLP-1 franchise is the most plausible agent of morbidity compression, which is the stated falsifier for the care-volume book. Owning it partially hedges the rest of the D sleeve. Cost: the entry price prices obesity for near-perfection.

Rate-side offset within the book: REITs in the hou vertical and spread insurers in the inc vertical sit on opposite sides of the limbs A-versus-E rate contradiction. Sized deliberately, that is a partial internal hedge rather than an accident.

TROW as the limb A control variable: held small, or simply tracked, as the instrument that tells you whether the flow reversal is showing up at all. If TROW's flows stabilise, limb A's premise is weaker than assumed.
RMD as the market's live GLP-1 pricing: the multiple is the cleanest read on how the market is currently pricing morbidity compression. Watch it whether or not you own it.
Private-pay weighting as the limb E hedge: the deliberate tilt toward hearing, ophthalmic premium, dental and death care is a structural hedge against reimbursement risk, not a separate theme.

clusters.title: Explicitly not owned
clusters.body: Named so the omissions are decisions rather than oversights.
items: Anything whose earnings depend on a government-set rate holding: the thesis's own success is the risk. Payors are tracked as limb E instruments, not held as limb D longs.
Pure labour arbitrage in care: businesses whose model is buying care labour cheaply and billing it dearly are on the wrong side of limb C. HCSG is a monitoring instrument, not a position.
The 'buy aging' basket: any position describable in three words has no edge in it. Large-cap diversified medtech (MDT) dilutes the demographic signal to nothing.
Levered senior housing operators as a core holding: BKD is genuinely binary between occupancy recovery and wage inflation. That is a trade, not a core position.
Raw materials and AI/semis exposure: covered by the sibling hard-assets-research and ai-hardware-research maps. Scope discipline is deliberate.

rules.body: Weakness w1 says demographics are the slowest variable in finance and a correct call can lose to carry for years. Default to expressions that are cash-generative or yielding. The labour-substitution sleeve is the deliberate exception — it is priced for growth and will not pay you to wait, so it is sized as the highest-conviction rather than the largest position.
Limb C and the substitution sleeve are one bet on one variable. Size them together as a single exposure to immigration policy, not as two independent positions.
Set an explicit ceiling on the share of the book whose earnings depend on a CMS or state Medicaid rate. Limb E is the reason the D-limb book tilts private-pay.
Do not let a net rate view emerge from the sum of the positions. State it, date it, size it separately — see weakness w2.
Run top-decile and median-retiree exposures as separate sleeves with separate theses. A single 'the retiree' framing produces wrong positions for one of them.

entry_windows.intro: Where the thesis is right and the price is not. Ranked by the gap between structural conviction and current crowding. These are watch conditions, not orders — the nightly robot flags when a drawdown threshold is crossed. Revised 2026-08-07: AMN removed after the filings showed revenue halved from peak and operating margin negative — a name cut to conviction 1 cannot simultaneously be an entry candidate. EME removed 2026-08-07 when falsifier f12 tripped — a sleeve the thesis has retired cannot head its entry list.

windows.setup: Best asset in the supply-trough trade, permanently expensive.
windows.watch: A rate back-up that hits REITs indiscriminately, or a labour-cost quarter that spooks the operating-portfolio structure.
windows.risk: It may simply never get cheap. The quality is real.

windows.setup: Owns accredited nursing capacity against 93,000 qualified applicants turned away in 2025. Re-based 2026-08-07: this is an APPLICANT-demand story, not a retirement-shortage one — BLS puts RN exit rates below baseline and employment growth at 4.9% a decade. Tuition is paid by students, and the filings back it (+9.9% revenue, +3.7pp margin).
windows.watch: Title IV and for-profit-education regulatory headlines, which are bimodal and recurrent — plus RN employment growth, now the thing that could soften applicant demand.
windows.risk: The regulatory tail is genuinely fat — size for it rather than hoping around it.

windows.setup: Cleanest private-pay age curve available; under-owned relative to reimbursed medtech.
windows.watch: An OTC hearing-aid scare that hits the whole complex, which has historically overshot.
windows.risk: Low-end commoditisation is a real long-run threat, not just a headline.

windows.setup: Cheapest way to own joint-replacement volume, discounted for genuine reasons.
windows.watch: Evidence that volume growth is finally outrunning price erosion, or a credible share stabilisation.
windows.risk: A decade of share loss is a pattern, not a discount.

avoid.title: Retired, not merely expensive
avoid.body: FIX, PWR, IESC and MYRG were previously held here as 'right thesis, wrong price'. As of 2026-08-07 that is no longer the position: falsifier f12 has tripped and the demographic premise under the contractor sleeve is refuted. They may well be good businesses — margins say they have pricing power — but this dashboard no longer has a claim on them, and holding them here would be borrowing the thesis's credibility for a bet it is not making.

catalyst_table.cats: Annual. Resets the depletion date and with it the entire limb E policy clock. The one scheduled event that most moves the fiscal limb.
Annual, winter. The tradable event for the payor vertical; the final Rate Announcement usually confirms it.
Quarterly. Occupancy, rate and starts — the direct read on limb H's supply-trough thesis. Read margin alongside occupancy.
Quarterly. The cleanest single confirmation or refutation of limb A's behavioural shift.
Annual. Tests the capacity-gap mechanism directly — applications turned away is the number that matters.
Monthly. Fast proxy for the labour shortage; use for direction only.
Monthly. The highest-value single indicator in the thesis — tests limb C's premise and limb D's timing at once.
Annual. Adjudicates limb B: whether the independent channel is actually taking share at the transfer break points.
Monthly. The consumption rotation, but only informative when normalised per capita by age band.
Irregular. Refreshes the cohort clock itself — the master time axis every other panel indexes to.

four_questions.q: What has to be true for this to work?
four_questions.a: That the age-band spending relay holds its historical shape, and that the labour pipeline stays capacity-constrained for longer than the market's implied adjustment period. Everything else is second order.

four_questions.q: What would make you exit entirely?
four_questions.a: A sustained immigration surge combined with 65+ participation continuing to climb. That is one coherent scenario and it neutralises limb C, most of limb D's cost-driven pricing, and the portfolio-construction conclusion in a single move.

Senior housing REITs and large-cap medtech — both fully narrativised. The crowd is thin in the labour limb, the intermediation limb and the median-retiree segment. Position sizing should reflect that, not the conviction ranking alone.

four_questions.q: What does this cost to hold?
four_questions.a: Most expressions are cash-generative or yielding by design. The labour-substitution sleeve is the exception and will not pay you to wait — hold it as the highest-conviction rather than the largest position.

repricings.title: Repriced 2026-08-07 — the per-capita utilisation finding
repricings.trigger: CMS data showed per-capita institutional utilisation falling 18-32% over 2014-2024 while ambulatory rose. See falsifier f11.
repricings.body: This does not change limb D's direction and it does not touch the age gradient, which came back steeper than assumed. It changes where inside limb D the money should sit. A business whose revenue is institutional days or admissions is levered to population growth MINUS a per-capita decline running at 3-4% a year. A business paid per ambulatory encounter, per hospice day, or by the patient directly is not.

moves.why: Revenue is admissions and days — precisely the measures in structural per-capita decline. Ensign remains the best operator in the sector and the operating-competence argument is untouched; what changes is that its end market grows far slower than the population chart suggests. Conviction on ENSG goes from 3 to 2 on magnitude, not on quality.

Rent coverage depends on tenant volumes. The landlord structure still insulates against limb C's wage inflation, which was the reason for owning them — but a slow-growing tenant end market weakens the long-run escalator story.

Hospice was the ONLY care category where per-capita utilisation rose over the decade, +21%. Terminal demand cannot be redirected to a cheaper site of care, deferred by better health management, or managed down by a payment model. That is exactly the property the rest of the care book has just been shown to lack.

E&M visits +16%, imaging +12%, procedures +5% per capita. Care is not disappearing, it is moving to the settings these businesses operate in. The site-of-care shift that hurts the institutional book is the same force that helps this one.

Unaffected by the finding entirely — no reimbursement rate, no payment model, no site-of-care substitution. The private-pay tilt was adopted as a hedge against limb E policy risk; it turns out to hedge this too. Raise its weight.

repricings.unchanged: The aging-in-place and personal-care names (ADUS, AVAH) sit largely outside this dataset — Medicaid-funded personal care is not in Medicare FFS utilisation at all. Their exposure is untested rather than confirmed safe, and that gap is now on the unsourced list.

repricings.title: Repriced 2026-08-07 (ii) — the wage split
repricings.trigger: BLS ECI showed care-labour wages running 3-9pp above baseline since 2019 while construction wages run below it. See falsifier f12.
repricings.body: Limb C was written as one claim and the data says it is two. Care labour scarcity is confirmed emphatically — service occupations, the category containing home health aides and nursing assistants, is the fastest-rising cut in the entire index at +9.2pp above baseline. Skilled construction trades are not confirmed at all: construction occupations run 0.7pp BELOW baseline and the construction industry 1.6pp below, both behind manufacturing. Two consequences, pulling opposite ways.

moves.why: The moat argument is that these firms own licensed labour that cannot be hired at any price. If that were binding, construction wages should be outpacing. They are the slowest cut on the board. These names were already froth-3 with no margin of safety on price; now the mechanism underneath them is unevidenced. Confound acknowledged: construction demand was soft over part of the window, so this could be a demand signal — but the thesis does not get to assume the reading that favours it.

Installation, maintenance and repair occupations run +3.0pp above baseline — the trades scarcity IS visible here, just not in construction. These three lean toward recurring service and maintenance rather than project construction, which is why they survive the finding while the pure construction names do not.

Service occupations +9.2pp and health care & social assistance +3.3pp above baseline. Whoever supplies or trains this labour has pricing power, and the capacity gap that creates it was independently confirmed by AACN's 93,000 turned-away applicants. This is now the best-evidenced part of the entire thesis.

Compounds iteration 1. These businesses face falling per-capita volumes AND the fastest-rising labour costs in the economy at once. The internal contradiction the matrix flagged as force 'wage' is no longer theoretical — it is measured, and it is the largest cost line in each of these P&Ls.

repricings.unchanged: Private-pay names are untouched again. Neither the utilisation finding nor the wage finding reaches ALC, SOON.SW, DEMANT.CO or STMN.SW, because none of them sells labour-intensive institutional care under a government rate.

repricings.title: Repriced 2026-08-07 (iii) — the filings correct me twice
repricings.trigger: SEC XBRL fundamentals for 110 of 126 names, CY2019-CY2025. Two of the previous four days' calls do not survive contact with the filed numbers.
repricings.body: This is the first iteration whose main output is reversing earlier work rather than adding to it. Both reversals come from the same mistake: reasoning from a correct macro finding straight to a company conclusion without checking whether the company behaved the way the sector did.

moves.why: Downgraded 3->2 in iteration 1 because per-capita SNF days are falling. The filings say Ensign compounded revenue 16.4% a year and expanded operating margin 2.1pp through exactly that decade. A consolidator in a fragmented sector can outgrow a shrinking per-capita market and this one did. Restored to 3; the utilisation finding is re-labelled a market-size warning.

Raised in iteration 2 on the logic that whoever supplies scarce labour has pricing power. False for agencies. AMN revenue fell from a $5.24bn peak to $2.73bn and operating margin swung 10pp into negative territory; CCRN -6.1pp and now filing to deregister. The shortage is real and it accrued to the employers, not the intermediaries. AMN cut to conviction 1.

Iteration 2 cut these because ECI wages showed no trades scarcity. Margins say otherwise: a median +5.1pp expansion on 10-42% revenue growth is pricing power however the wages behaved. The moat may be contractor capacity rather than labour cost. Reduction stands for the pure-construction names on valuation, but not on 'the mechanism is absent'.

moves.n: Care-labour TRAINING, as distinct from supply
moves.why: The one care-labour name the filings support: +9.9% revenue CAGR with margin +3.7pp. Owning accredited capacity behaves completely differently from renting out staff. Note the ticker — Adtalem renamed to Covista in 2026 and the universe was carrying the stale symbol until this run caught it.

The automation sleeve is the highest-carry position in the book, explicitly priced for growth and explicitly not paying you to wait. Median revenue CAGR is 3.7%, the weakest of ten verticals, with margins slightly down. Six years is long enough that 'the substitution capex is coming' needs evidence, and there is none in the filings.

repricings.unchanged: Private-pay again untouched — but note that most of that sleeve (SOON.SW, DEMANT.CO, ALC, STMN.SW) files outside the US and therefore cannot be tested this way at all. Sixteen names have no SEC filings; their calls remain judgment-only.

repricings.title: Repriced 2026-08-07 (iv) — f12 tripped, and the care scarcity relocates
repricings.trigger: BLS labour force exit rates by occupation. Trades exit BELOW the all-occupation baseline; care aides exit far above it. Falsifier f12 moved warming -> tripped.
repricings.body: A falsifier written in advance has tripped, so the positions it named come off — that is the whole point of writing it down before the money was at risk. But the same data relocates the care-labour scarcity to a different occupation than the thesis assumed, which changes two other calls.

moves.why: Three independent reads now. Wages: construction below the all-civilian baseline. Exit rates: 2.8-3.2% against a 4.7% baseline, so the trades are ageing out SLOWER than the workforce. Margins: expanding — the one supportive read, and equally explicable by a datacentre construction cycle. The demographic premise under this sleeve is refuted on the measure that tests it most directly. These may still be good businesses; they are no longer boomerification businesses, and this dashboard has no claim on them.

moves.n: The real care-labour crunch — aide-employing operators
moves.why: Home health and personal care aides have an 8.6% annual exit rate — the highest of any occupation examined, nearly double the baseline — with annual openings equal to 17.6% of employment and demand growing 17% over the decade. That is the single most acute labour scarcity in the thesis and these companies sit directly in it. Crucially the filings show they are handling it: ADUS margin +4.3pp and AVAH +7.7pp over CY2019-CY2025 while employing the highest-churn occupation in the economy. The cost risk is real and demonstrably managed, which is a competence signal rather than a warning.

An awkward finding for a position raised only hours ago. BLS puts registered-nurse employment growth at 4.9% over the decade with a below-baseline 2.8% exit rate — so the 'nursing shortage' is not the retirement story the thesis told. The education case survives on a different footing: AACN's 93,000 turned-away applicants is measured APPLICANT demand, and tuition is paid by students, not by the employment market. CVSA's filings back it (+9.9% revenue, +3.7pp margin). Holding at 3, but the reasoning is re-based from labour scarcity to applicant demand, and if RN employment growth stays this modest, tuition demand is the thing to watch.

repricings.unchanged: Nothing in limbs A, B, D, E or H is touched. This is a limb C event, and limb C is now conviction 2 rather than 3 — of the three occupational groups it claimed, only care support survives testing.

repricings.title: Repriced 2026-08-07 (v) — the personal-care payer confirms, on volume only
repricings.trigger: CMS Medicaid data. HCBS waiver penetration among 65+ rose 8.31% to 10.66% in two years, and LTSS enrolment grew through the unwinding while total Medicaid fell 13%.
repricings.body: Iteration 4 raised ADUS and AVAH into the highest-churn labour market in the country without having tested who pays them. That gap is now closed on the demand side and it closes favourably — but only on the demand side, and the distinction is the whole point of this entry.

moves.n: Confirmed — Medicaid is rebalancing toward home care
moves.why: Waiver enrolment among 65+ grew nearly three times faster than eligibility, and LTSS enrolment ROSE 7.7% across 2023-24 while total Medicaid managed care fell 13%. The aged and disabled LTSS population is categorically eligible and was insulated from the unwinding that removed millions of working-age adults. This is the payer moving deliberately toward the service these companies sell, and it corroborates the site-of-care shift found in the Medicare data from an entirely separate dataset.

moves.n: But the rate side is unobservable
moves.why: Everything above measures VOLUME. Medicaid LTSS expenditure reporting — the rate side — stops at FY2020 and is published as PDF. Rates have always been the real risk to these operators, not volumes, and at zero cost that risk cannot be tracked. The position is confirmed on the half that is observable and blind on the half that matters more. Sized accordingly rather than raised further.

repricings.unchanged: This says nothing about the SNF operators — Medicaid rebalancing toward home care is, if anything, the other side of the institutional decline found in iteration 1.

repricings.title: Repriced 2026-08-07 (vi) — the untested sleeve tests worst
repricings.trigger: First-ever fundamentals check on the 10 non-SEC filers. Median revenue CAGR 4.2%, median margin -1.3pp.
repricings.body: The private-pay sleeve had survived every finding in this programme for a reason that should have been obvious earlier: no evidence had ever reached it. Sixteen names filed outside the SEC and were therefore exempt from the filings pass that corrected two calls in iteration 3. Covered now via vendor income statements — lower provenance, shorter spans — and the result is the weakest set of numbers in the book.

moves.why: Sonova revenue CAGR -1.2% and margin -1.3pp over FY2023-26; Amplifon +4.2% revenue but margin -4.1pp. A conviction-3 core position should not be shrinking. SOON.SW cut to 2. Caveats stated rather than leaned on: three-year window, post-COVID normalisation, and a strengthening reporting currency against global earnings.

Cochlear +12.4% revenue CAGR is the only name in the sleeve where the demographic story shows up in the numbers, and Demant is the only one with expanding margin (+1.4pp). Both were held at 2 on valuation; the numbers support the thesis, the prices still do not.

Unicharm +1.7% revenue with margin -2.0pp; Fanuc +0.2% and -1.1pp. These were always held more for what they reveal about the demographic transition than for their returns, and the numbers confirm that reading. Keep as instruments, not positions.

repricings.unchanged: ALC, the largest private-pay name, files a 20-F and was already in the SEC set — its numbers are unaffected by this.
